title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: A margin you cannot trace to an invoice and a collection date is only an opinion.
epigraph.author: Underwriting Rule

web_blocks.html: MPS sells directly, to enterprises, and almost entirely abroad. Of ₹768.36 Cr of FY26 revenue, ₹764.83 Cr was exports and ₹3.54 Cr was domestic [1]. There are no distributors or retail channels. Management describes a ‘captive base of 1,100 or more customers, many held for two decades’ [1]. New logos come through a central growth engine [1]. In Q4 FY25 the CEO described the commercial model as five prongs. The first is a revised go-to-market that sells firm-wide capabilities rather than individual products. The second is a heavier emphasis on ‘star accounts’, meaning cross-sell and up-sell. The third is new customers in every segment. The fourth is new capabilities such as DigiCore Pro. The fifth is fast integration of AJE [20, 10]. Relationships are executive-sponsored. On the Q2 FY25 call Rahul Arora said he personally sponsors the Springer Nature mandate. Springer Nature’s chief operating officer is his counterpart [8]. Selling is therefore account management at the top of the customer, plus RFPs when a customer consolidates its vendors.

web_blocks.caption: Go-to-market, delivery and billing by channel (what the record shows, and what is inferred)
web_blocks.takeaway: Channels differ sharply in billing rhythm. Subscription and platform revenue is billed ahead of service, which is why contract liabilities (₹122.97 Cr) are almost as large as trade receivables (₹133.48 Cr). Project work is billed on milestones, which is why contract assets exist (₹58.30 Cr). Sales-cycle lengths are management’s qualitative statements where quoted; the record does not disclose RFP-to-award durations, and we mark inferences as such [1, 2].

web_blocks.html: How contracts are structured and renewed. The CEO told the Q2 FY27 call that research contracts ‘tend to be three to five years, tend to be long-term’. He said the lifecycle has not changed with AI [2]. The annual report calls the company’s defence against insourcing and client concentration ‘structural rather than contractual’. It points to relationships measured in decades, platforms customers run daily operations on, and switching costs [1]. We read that two ways. As an investor you get long contracts and sticky platforms. You also get a price reset once every three to five years, against a customer who has just watched AI cut production effort. The renewal is where the AI gain is actually divided. The record describes tenor and stickiness, not the legal form (master services agreement, statements of work, preferred-vendor status). Where management has discussed it, the vocabulary is ‘vendor consolidation’ and ‘global agreements’. In Q2 FY25 the CEO said the China presence lets MPS take part in global agreements with customers who had to compromise on their preferred-vendor strategy there [8]. In Q2 FY26 David Goodman, who presented Education, said MPS was succeeding in vendor consolidation [17].

How a new client is qualified. Large publishers and enterprises audit suppliers before handing over unpublished manuscripts, student records or learner data. MPS lists ISO 9001:2015, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, PCI-DSS, GDPR compliance and COUNTER 5 compliance in the annual report [1]. In September 2026 it added ISO 42001, the international standard for governing AI. Customers can now audit its AI use ‘the way they audit us for security’ [2]. The second qualification is the pilot. In Q3 FY25 management reported completing and delivering pilot projects with new logos [22]. In Q3 FY26 David Goodman, who leads MPS North America, said successful pilots with major K-12 and higher-education customers were converting into follow-on waves [18]. In Q4 FY25 management said the e-learning solutions being pitched were more complex and needed more iterated testing and piloting. That is one reason deals closed slower than expected [20].

web_blocks.caption: Worked client win: from vendor-consolidation RFP to steady-state billing (the 2026 publisher mandates)
web_blocks.takeaway: The 2026 mandates show the ramp economics. MPS hires ahead of billing, which is a cost drag. Billing begins within weeks to months of award, and margin should recover as the work reaches steady state. First-half FY27 revenue was nearly flat sequentially, at ₹224.24 Cr in Q1 and about ₹224 Cr in Q2. EBITDA margin stayed at 34.3% in both quarters. That is what an investment-phase ramp looks like when operating leverage elsewhere protects the cost base [25, 2, 36].

web_blocks.html: A second, smaller win from the record is the HighWire platform. In Q2 FY25 Tony Alves, the senior vice president of product management, said MPS won a new logo away from its largest content-hosting competitor. He also saw ‘an influx of activity in new RFIs and RFPs’. His argument was that HighWire and MPS offer the only serious independent choice, because the alternatives are publisher- or private-equity-owned [8]. Hosting wins are slower and stickier than production wins. The customer’s content, usage data and subscriber logins move onto the platform. That is why the AR leans on ‘platforms our customers run their daily operations on’ as the moat [1].

Where the work is delivered from. MPS reports more than 3,200 colleagues in nine countries on four continents. It runs 15 delivery centres [1]. The primary Indian centres named in the annual report are Dehradun, Bengaluru, Chennai, Mumbai and Noida. The corporate note adds Gurugram. Production facilities are listed in Chennai, Noida, Mumbai, Dehradun, Gurugram and Bengaluru [1]. Pune does not appear as an MPS site in the record. It is the statutory auditor’s signing place. Outside India the MPS site lists US offices in Winter Park, Florida (MPS North America), Media, Pennsylvania (Unbound Medicine) and Princeton, New Jersey. It also lists Beijing for AJE’s Chinese entity, Singapore, Tübingen in Germany (TOPSIM), Baar in Switzerland (MPS Europa), Oxford in the UK (Semantico), Melbourne (Liberate Learning) and Woodbridge, Ontario [33]. Growth, sales and delivery leaders joined the calls from Austin, Texas, Noida, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Singapore [17, 2]. The AR describes a presence in smaller Indian cities as a cost advantage with a deep and loyal talent base [1].

web_blocks.caption: People economics and cost structure, FY25 to FY26 (consolidated, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: The cost base is a payroll plus a variable layer of external contractors. Employee cost fell 2.4% in absolute terms in FY26 while revenue grew 5.7%, taking it from 45.1% to 41.6% of revenue; outsourcing (copy-editing, authoring, conversion, typesetting, media arts) rose to 14.9% of revenue. Attrition of permanent employees at the listed entity rose to 28.85%, which is a real execution risk behind the margin gains. Per-head figures use ‘more than 3,200’ as a floor for year-end headcount and are therefore approximate (computed) [1, 24].

web_blocks.html: The people economics have a second layer that is easy to miss. MPS Labs, the AI and engineering group, is about 250 to 300 people. That is separate from a platforms team of about 300 [17]. The CEO told the Q2 FY27 call that more than 200 engineers build the AI in-house. He also said ‘we don’t capitalize our expenses at all’ [2]. The audited cash flow statement agrees. Capital expenditure on intangible assets under development was only ₹0.21 Cr in FY26 [1]. That makes reported EBITDA cleaner than at companies that capitalise product development. It also means engineering investment is already inside the 30.7% margin.

Pricing mechanics. The annual report’s revenue policy lists three models. Fixed-price contracts are recognised on a percentage-of-completion basis using effort incurred. Time-and-material and job contracts are recognised on an output basis, such as units delivered, effort expended or transactions processed. Fixed-price maintenance is recognised straight-line over time [1]. Revenue is measured net of volume discounts, service-level credits, performance bonuses and price concessions. In FY26 contracted price of ₹772.80 Cr became revenue of ₹768.36 Cr after ₹4.43 Cr (0.57%) of such deductions [1]. Management describes commercial layers on top of that. One is per-unit production pricing (page, article, title, submission). Another is subscriptions (Unbound, THINK365, hosting). A third is AJE’s consumer price list, from $13 for English editing to $420 for scientific editing, with $289 for pre-submission review [28]. A fourth is a growing share of ‘outcome-based’ revenue. Management put that at 25% of revenue, with recurring revenue at 45%, on the Q1 FY27 call [25]. The group says pricing pressure is a ‘constant risk’. It handles that by trading price for volume and through automation [1]. We cannot see rate cards. The evidence for pricing power is therefore indirect: Unbound’s annual increases and the stability of reported margins while volume grows.

Billing and collection. The revenue note says trade receivables are non-interest-bearing and generally on terms of 0 to 60 days [1]. Trade receivables stood at ₹133.48 Cr at 31 March 2026, against ₹116.58 Cr a year earlier. They include ₹17.62 Cr of unbilled amounts. Ageing shows 65.9% not yet due, 18.4% under six months past due and 2.6% (₹3.58 Cr) over a year past due. The credit-loss allowance is ₹4.30 Cr, or 3.1% of gross receivables (all computed from the ageing table) [1]. Management’s own DSO measure was 51 days at the end of March 2026, 45 at the end of June and 38 at the end of September. The CFO said on the Q2 FY27 call that ‘DSO came down to 38 days from 45 at the end of June’ [25, 2]. The simple closing-receivables measure (receivables divided by revenue times 365) gives about 63 days for FY26 (computed). That equals the aggregator’s 63 days [1, 36]. The company’s own formula shows 51 days, and its definition is not published. We treat 51 versus 63 as a definitional gap, not a discrepancy.

web_blocks.caption: Contract balances: customers fund the working capital (consolidated, ₹ Cr, 31 March)
web_blocks.takeaway: Receivables plus unbilled contract assets less customer prepayments (contract liabilities) is only ₹68.81 Cr at 31 March 2026. That is about 33 days of revenue (computed), versus about 33.5 days a year earlier. Advances and subscription billing fund about two-thirds of the receivables book. But FY26’s contract-liability balance was lifted by ₹34.98 Cr acquired with Unbound. Excluding it, the balance fell from ₹98.79 Cr to about ₹87.99 Cr, partly because AJE advances were written back. Treat the customer-funded position as real but not growing on its own [1].

web_blocks.html: Forex: dollars and pounds in, rupees out. Nearly all revenue is billed in foreign currency. A large share of the cost base (Indian payroll, rent, subcontractors) is in rupees [1]. The annual report’s financial-risk note quantifies only the balance-sheet exposure. It says its sensitivity ‘ignores any impact on forecast revenue and expenses’ [1]. Net balance-sheet exposure at 31 March 2026 was ₹113.93 Cr in US dollars. That is ₹79.89 Cr of receivables, a ₹25.51 Cr intercompany loan and ₹9.13 Cr of cash. Euro exposure was ₹3.04 Cr and pound exposure ₹5.72 Cr. Other currencies were a net liability of ₹22.95 Cr, mostly acquisition-related financial liabilities. A 1% move in the US dollar changes pre-tax profit by ₹1.14 Cr. The euro moves it by ₹0.03 Cr and the pound by ₹0.06 Cr [1]. The operating exposure is far larger. US customers alone were ₹327.80 Cr of FY26 revenue. As an upper bound that ignores hedges and foreign-currency costs, every 1% rupee move against the dollar shifts revenue by about ₹3.28 Cr. That is roughly 1.4% of FY26 EBITDA (our illustration, computed). Management’s defences are hedging and planning rates. The risk table says the company freezes planning rates in two-year cycles and takes ‘adequate hedging’ [1]. The CFO said on the Q2 FY27 call that ‘because we plan the business at an exchange rate well below today’s, the new floor does not depend on the currency’ [2]. Forward contracts outstanding at year-end were forward sales of US$8.10 million for ₹74.32 Cr, an average of about ₹91.75 a dollar (computed). They also included £0.40 million for ₹4.85 Cr. A year earlier the figures were US$4.70 million and £0.50 million. The cash flow statement shows an unrealised mark-to-market loss of ₹3.65 Cr on those forwards [1]. Translation also mattered. The foreign-currency translation reserve gained ₹28.97 Cr in FY26. That flows through other comprehensive income, not profit [1].

web_blocks.caption: Currency exposure and sensitivity (annual report Note 34, ₹ Cr unless stated)
web_blocks.takeaway: The disclosed balance-sheet sensitivity is small, at ₹1.14 Cr per 1% in the dollar. The revenue-side sensitivity is bigger and is not quantified in the audited note. The forward book covers about 65% of the net dollar balance-sheet exposure on paper (rupee notional against rupee exposure, computed). It does not address revenue sensitivity. The real protection is that MPS plans at a rate it says is well below the current one [1, 2].

web_blocks.caption: MPS Limited: Worked ₹100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall (audited FY26 consolidated, year ended 31 March 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue, ₹56.50 went to people and subcontractors and ₹12.80 to other operating costs. That left ₹30.69 of EBITDA. After ₹3.61 of depreciation and amortisation, ₹0.26 of interest, ₹2.03 of other income, ₹0.99 of net exceptional gains and ₹7.30 of tax, ₹22.54 reached profit after tax. Operating cash flow was ₹25.61 per ₹100, which is 83% of EBITDA and 114% of PAT. With only ₹1.10 of capital expenditure and ₹0.62 of lease payments, free cash flow after leases was ₹23.89 per ₹100. That is before ₹16.93 per ₹100 spent on acquisitions (mainly Unbound). FY26 profit before tax includes ₹7.64 Cr of net exceptional items. About ₹0.99 of the ₹29.84 of PBT per ₹100 is therefore non-recurring.

web_blocks.html: Reconciliation to the blind snapshot. The aggregator’s FY26 line shows sales ₹768 Cr, expenses ₹533 Cr and operating profit ₹236 Cr. It shows other income ₹23 Cr, interest ₹2 Cr, depreciation ₹28 Cr and PBT ₹229 Cr. Net profit is ₹173 Cr, operating cash flow ₹197 Cr and investing cash flow -₹132 Cr [36]. It ties to the audited statements. The aggregator’s ₹23 Cr of other income is our ₹15.58 Cr plus ₹7.64 Cr of net exceptional items (₹23.22 Cr). Its ₹533 Cr of expenses is employee cost plus other expenses (₹532.52 Cr). Its investing outflow of ₹132 Cr is the audited ₹132.87 Cr. That is dominated by ₹130.06 Cr paid for acquisitions (Unbound and the remaining Liberate stake) [1]. The aggregator’s free cash flow of ₹188 Cr equals our CFO less capex. The only differences are rounding and the grouping of exceptional items inside other income. One difference of definition matters for cash conversion. The aggregator’s CFO-to-EBITDA ratio of 103% is measured before tax. Our 83% uses cash flow after ₹46.66 Cr of tax paid.

Reading the waterfall. Three things stand out. First, FY26’s cash conversion was good in a year when it could have been poor. FY25’s operating cash flow was only ₹100.90 Cr against PAT of ₹148.91 Cr. That is 68% of PAT and 48% of EBITDA. ₹64.40 Cr of working capital unwound, from acquired AJE liabilities and customer advances running off. In FY26 that drag was gone [1]. Second, the business is capital-light. ₹8.47 Cr of capex is 1.1% of revenue, and software development is expensed. The uses of cash are acquisitions and dividends, not capex. In FY26 MPS spent ₹130.06 Cr on acquisitions (mainly Unbound, net of cash acquired). It paid ₹86.69 Cr of dividends and drew ₹42.00 Cr of term loans. Borrowings ended at ₹40.25 Cr. Management said it repaid them in full in August 2026, leaving ₹163 Cr of cash and no debt at 30 September 2026 [1, 2]. Third, the CEO said on the Q1 FY27 call that ‘the business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month’. That is consistent with FY26’s ₹183.56 Cr of free cash flow after leases, or about ₹15.3 Cr a month (computed) [25, 1].

web_blocks.company: Appen Limited (ASX-listed AI training-data and annotation services)
web_blocks.mechanism: A people-plus-technology services vendor had a largest customer worth roughly 30% of revenue. That customer terminated its contract during FY24. The division that served it shrank by more than a third in a single year. The company recovered only because the rest of its book was growing and because it cut operating costs. The lost client did not come back.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: FY23 revenue was US$273.0 million. About US$82.6 million of it came from the largest customer. That figure sums the four FY23 quarters in the company’s results presentation: 19.1, 18.3, 21.9 and 23.3. FY24 revenue from that customer was US$13.4 million. Total revenue fell 14% to US$234.3 million. The Global Services division fell 38%, from US$191.5 million to US$118.1 million. Revenue excluding that customer rose 16% to US$220.9 million. Operating expenses were cut 26%. Underlying EBITDA before FX moved from -US$20.4 million to +US$3.5 million.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: MPS’s largest customer was 17.3% of FY26 revenue, and its top five were about 46% of revenue in Q2 FY27. A one-client shock of Appen’s size (30%) is therefore larger than anything in MPS’s disclosed book. MPS’s large relationships run on contracts that the CEO says typically last three to five years, with platforms embedded in customer workflows. We have not verified how Appen’s contract was structured. The transferable lesson is about speed. Customers decide on their own procurement calendar. A services business with a largely people-based cost base pays for that decision within two quarters. Appen’s recovery came from diversification (revenue excluding the lost client up 16%) and from cost-out (operating expenses down 26%). At MPS, watch the top-five share. Also watch how much of the payroll can flex through the contractor and gig layer visible in the ₹114.21 Cr outsourcing line [37, 1, 2].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: Who funds the working capital?
paragraphs: Most services companies we study have a receivables problem: they do the work, they wait, and growth eats cash. MPS looks different because its balance sheet is partly customer-funded. Contract liabilities of ₹122.97 Cr nearly match trade receivables of ₹133.48 Cr, and the net position of ₹68.81 Cr is about 33 days of revenue. That is why FY26 cash conversion was strong even as the company grew.

The honest qualifier is that this cushion is partly acquired (Unbound’s ₹34.98 Cr of deferred revenue) and partly management’s policy choices (AJE advances were written back after a change in policy). If you are tracking MPS’s cash quality, watch contract liabilities excluding acquisitions, not just DSO.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: The cost line nobody headlines
paragraphs: The headline cost is payroll: ₹319.95 Cr, 41.6% of revenue. The second-largest line is almost never discussed: ₹114.21 Cr of outsourcing, 14.9% of revenue, paid to sub-contractors for copy-editing, authoring, conversion, typesetting and media arts. That is a variable cost layer, and it is where MPS’s ‘gig and associate’ strategy shows up. It is also the layer that generative AI attacks first, because it is the most standardised work.

So when management says AI is reducing effort, the first place to look is whether outsourcing grows slower than revenue. In FY26 it grew 9.7% against revenue growth of 5.7%, which means AI has not yet reduced the external layer. The payroll fell instead, helped by AJE offshoring and the Corporate Learning restructuring. That is a fact about FY26, and the next two years of the same line will say more than any call.

web_blocks.html: What is weak in the unit economics. We see four soft spots. The first is attrition. Permanent-employee turnover at the listed entity rose from 19.4% to 28.85% in a year. At that level, hiring and training costs and delivery quality become real issues [1]. The second is the ramp. New mandates require hiring ahead, and Q2 FY27 revenue was nearly flat sequentially for that reason. The margin held at 34.3%, but it depends on those mandates reaching steady state in H2 [2]. The third is concentration. About 58% of revenue from 15 customers means a single renewal negotiation can move the margin. The fourth is the quality of recent profit. ₹7.64 Cr of the FY26 PBT is exceptional, and ₹6.40 Cr of other income is a write-back of liabilities no longer required. About ₹14 Cr of FY26 PBT is therefore not operating profit [1]. None of these breaks the model. The unit economics are strong, with capex of 1.1% of revenue, free cash flow near 24% of revenue and no debt at September 2026. But these are the places where we would look first for a miss.

What would change our view of unit economics (business triggers only). The first trigger is free cash flow after lease payments falling below about 80% of PAT for two consecutive years. The second is attrition staying above 25% while the sub-contractor cost line grows faster than revenue. The third is contract liabilities, excluding acquisitions, shrinking for a second year. The fourth is a top-five client share moving back above 50% on the audited basis.

book_paragraphs: Imagine you are sitting in the procurement office of a large scientific publisher. A stack of submissions is arriving that is ten times what your editorial offices were built for, some of it written by machines and some of it by fraud rings. Your job is to pick the few partners who can take this work without losing a day or leaking a manuscript. You will talk to five or six vendors, ask each for audits and certificates, and run pilots on live batches. You will not give the work to a stranger. That, in a paragraph, is how MPS sells. There are no distributors and no shop windows. Nearly all of MPS’s revenue is billed to customers outside India, and the relationships are with executives who know each other: the CEO says he personally sponsors the Springer Nature mandate, with that company’s chief operating officer on the other side.

What do those customers buy, and for how long? The CEO told the Q2 FY27 call that contracts in research ‘tend to be three to five years, tend to be long-term’. That sounds like a fortress, and in part it is, because the platforms MPS hosts store a customer’s content and subscribers. But I want you to notice the other side of a three-to-five-year contract. Once in that cycle the customer sits down to renegotiate, and it has just watched AI cut the effort that production takes. That renewal is where the productivity gain is divided. Nothing in the filings lets us see a single price-per-unit, so we judge indirectly, by margins, by Unbound’s annual price rises, and by the stability of the contract base.

Let me walk through a win, using the one the company has described this year. A top-five publisher gives MPS a large production mandate and a research-integrity mandate, and moves more than 110,000 submissions a year onto MPS’s peer-review platform. The calendar tells you something. The mandates were won in the July-to-September quarter, they begin to bill in November and December, and meanwhile MPS hires ahead of the work. So for a few months you pay for people before you get paid for outputs. Revenue in the second quarter was almost flat compared with the first, and the CEO explained it to a questioning analyst as timing, saying the larger mandates ‘only start billing in November and December’. Notice that the margin did not fall; it held at 34.3%, which tells you the existing base was carrying the cost of the ramp.

Where does the work get done? Mostly in India, in Noida, Dehradun, Chennai, Bengaluru, Mumbai and Gurugram, with sales and engineering outposts in Florida, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Austin, Oxford, Tübingen, Baar, Melbourne, Beijing and Singapore. Pune, which a casual reader might expect, is not on the list; it is where the auditor signs. About 3,200 people carry the whole company. If you divide revenue by headcount you get roughly ₹24 lakh per person, payroll of ₹10 lakh and an EBITDA of ₹7.4 lakh per person. Those are not software-like numbers, and they should not be: this is a people-plus-platform business. What I find more interesting is the layer beside the payroll, the ₹114 crore that MPS pays to sub-contractors for copy-editing, typesetting and media work. It is nearly 15% of revenue and it is where a flexible workforce shows up.

Now to cash, where this business is more interesting than most services companies. Look at the balance sheet at the end of March 2026. Customers owed MPS ₹133 crore of receivables, and MPS owed its customers ₹123 crore of services already billed but not yet delivered, the contract liabilities. Add the ₹58 crore of work done but not yet invoiced, and the net working-capital position is only ₹69 crore, about 33 days of revenue. The CFO said in November that the company’s own measure of days of receivables ‘came down to 38 days from 45 at the end of June’. Subscriptions billed in advance, platform fees and customer advances are doing a lot of the financing. One caution: part of that cushion arrived with the Unbound acquisition, and part came from a decision to write back some old AJE customer advances.

The other thing you must understand is money in and money out. MPS earns in dollars, pounds and euros and spends mostly in rupees. The annual report discloses only the balance-sheet side: a 1% move in the dollar changes pre-tax profit by about ₹1.14 crore. The far bigger exposure is operating, because US customers alone were ₹328 crore of revenue. As an upper bound, a 1% rupee move shifts about ₹3.3 crore of revenue, roughly 1.4% of EBITDA. The company hedges, with forward sales of US$8.1 million outstanding at an average rate of about ₹91.75, and plans its budgets at an exchange rate it says is well below today’s. The CFO said that ‘because we plan the business at an exchange rate well below today’s, the new floor does not depend on the currency.’ That is the right way to run an exporter. It is also a reminder that margin gains of recent years have been helped by a weaker rupee, and that the sensitivity is real even if the audited note does not quantify it.

Now to the ₹100 waterfall, which I would like you to keep in your head. Of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue, ₹41.64 went to employees, ₹14.86 to sub-contractors and ₹12.80 to everything else operating, leaving ₹30.69 of EBITDA. Depreciation took ₹3.61, tax ₹7.30, and ₹22.54 of profit was left. Cash from operations was ₹25.61, because depreciation is not cash and working capital was neutral. Capex was ₹1.10 and lease payments ₹0.62, so free cash flow after leases was ₹23.89. In the same year, MPS spent ₹130 crore on acquisitions, mainly Unbound, and ₹87 crore on dividends, and still ended the year in a net cash position.

How does a company with a small revenue gain produce a big profit gain? The CFO had a plain answer on the Q2 FY27 call: ‘Over the last six quarters, revenue grew about 20% and EBITDA grew about 53%. That gap is operating leverage.’ In FY26, the audited numbers show what that gap is made of. Revenue rose by ₹41 crore, employee cost fell by ₹8 crore, and other expenses (mostly sub-contractors and software) rose by ₹25 crore, so EBITDA rose by about ₹25 crore. The CEO’s cash remark follows from the same arithmetic: on the Q1 FY27 call he said ‘the business is throwing out INR15 crores to INR18 crores of cash every month.’ My own check, dividing the ₹183.56 crore of free cash flow after leases by twelve, gives about ₹15 crore a month, so the claim sits at the low end of his range, not above it. I find that reassuring.

Is there a cautionary tale for a business like this? Yes, and it is not a famous one. Appen, an Australian data-annotation services company, had one customer that was about 30% of FY23 revenue. When that customer ended its contract, revenue fell 14% in a year and its largest division fell 38%. The company survived because its other work was growing and because it cut costs. MPS’s largest customer is 17% of revenue, its top five about 46%, and its contracts are longer and more embedded. That is better, but ‘better than Appen’ is a low bar. The lesson I take is about speed: when a customer decides, the bill arrives in the next two quarters.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION: Customers pay first
book_callouts.quote: The most important cash fact about MPS is not how much it earns, but who funds the gap between work done and cash received.
book_callouts.text: At 31 March 2026 MPS had ₹123 crore of customer prepayments against ₹133 crore of receivables. That is an unusual position for a services business, and it explains why free cash flow after leases reached 24% of revenue. It also means the cash quality depends on keeping the subscriptions, the platform fees and the advances coming, so the trend in contract liabilities belongs on your dashboard next to DSO.
bullets: Receivables ₹133.48 crore; contract liabilities ₹122.97 crore; contract assets ₹58.30 crore; net position about 33 days of revenue.
₹34.98 crore of the contract liabilities arrived with Unbound; AJE advances of ₹13.95 crore were written back in FY26.
Free cash flow after lease payments: ₹183.56 crore, or ₹23.89 per ₹100 of revenue.

book_subsections.title: From RFP to steady state: the anatomy of a win
paragraphs: I like to break a client win into seven stages, because each stage has a different cash and margin effect. The trigger is a customer consolidating vendors. Qualification means audits and pilots, and MPS carries the certificates that open the door: ISO 9001, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, GDPR, COUNTER 5, and, since September 2026, ISO 42001 for AI governance. Award is the multi-year mandate. Then comes the awkward part, hiring ahead of billing, followed by go-live, steady state and, years later, a renewal where the price is reset.

In the current wave, the company told us that hiring is done and billing starts in November and December. It said the second half is about bringing the mandates to a steady state while holding the margin. That is a promise we can check in the Q3 and Q4 results. If the margin holds while revenue steps up, the model works the way management says. If the margin dips as billing starts, we will learn that the ramp is heavier than described.

book_subsections.title: The people question behind the margin
paragraphs: Here is the number I would put on a card on my desk: 28.85%. That is the attrition rate for permanent employees at the listed company in FY26, up from 19.4% the year before and 18% the year before that. The company has been cutting people in some places, with Corporate Learning headcount about a third lower and AJE’s US roles all moved to India, so part of that figure is by design. But in an industry where the deliverable is accuracy, a rising departure rate can quietly turn into rework, and rework turns into margin leakage.

The CEO says that net promoter scores went up, not down, through the AJE transition, and the audited cost numbers show employee costs falling while revenue rises. I take both at face value. What I would ask in the next call is how attrition looks by segment and what tenure the leavers had. The data we have does not answer it.

One more point on people. The company says it does not capitalise its development spending, and the cash flow statement agrees. That means the 250 to 300 people in MPS Labs and the 300 on the platforms team are charged to the profit and loss statement in the year they work, so the 30.7% EBITDA margin is after paying for the future, not before it.

book_subsections.title: What a good unit-economics year looks like, and what a bad one would be
paragraphs: A good year for MPS looks like FY26: revenue up a little, payroll down a little, EBITDA margin up 170 basis points, cash conversion above 80% of EBITDA, almost nothing spent on capex, and a rising pile of cash even after an acquisition and a full dividend cycle. A bad year would look different in specific ways. Contract liabilities would shrink without an obvious one-off reason. The sub-contractor line would rise faster than revenue even as management said AI was cutting effort. Attrition would stay high. And one of the five biggest customers would rebid its contract.

I will leave you with the rule I use for businesses like this one. Follow the invoice. Who gets it, how often, how large, and when does the cash arrive? For MPS the answers are encouraging for FY26 and still unproven for the first big renewal after the AI cost cuts.
